query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding approximately 6 at.% germanium to a titanium‐ and nickel‐primary high‐entropy alloy refines its microstructure and promotes the formation of stable, protective phases during elevated-temperature exposure, thereby improving its high-temperature mechanical properties relative to the same alloy without germanium.
generation.material_initial_state: A titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy composed of five or more elements (each 5–35 at%) with titanium and nickel as the primary constituents, processed by methods such as DED.
generation.intervention: Introduce ~6 at.% germanium into the alloy’s composition during fabrication.
generation.conditions: The alloy will be subjected to elevated-temperature conditions representative of its intended extreme environment applications.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined grain microstructure with stabilized protective phase precipitates (e.g., refined silicide or oxide scales) that form during high-temperature exposure.
generation.mechanism: Germanium is expected to act as a microstructure refiner and phase stabilizer, similar to observations in Nb-Ti-Si-based systems. It refines the grain size and promotes the formation of continuous, protective phases that can inhibit oxidation and improve load transfer under high-temperature conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: The germanium-alloyed high-entropy alloy will exhibit improved high-temperature yield strength, hardness, and oxidation resistance compared to the baseline alloy without the germanium addition.
generation.baseline: The titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy manufactured without germanium.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable for high-entropy alloys where titanium and nickel are primary constituents and within the compositional limits of 5–35 at% for each element. It is assumed that the fabrication method (e.g., DED or similar rapid solidification techniques) is maintained constant between test and control samples.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative magnitude of the improvement in mechanical properties and the full extent of the phase transformations promoted by germanium require experimental confirmation. Variations in processing parameters or the presence of additional minor elements could also influence the outcome.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy samples using identical processing conditions (e.g., direct energy deposition). One set should incorporate ~6 at.% germanium while the control set does not. Subject both sets to identical elevated-temperature mechanical testing and oxidation experiments.
measurements: Microstructure characterization (grain size analysis, phase identification via XRD/SEM/EDS)
Oxidation resistance (scale thickness and weight gain after exposure)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the germanium-containing alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement (for example, less than a 10–15% increase in high-temperature strength, hardness, or oxidation resistance) relative to the control alloy under identical testing conditions, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The addition of Ge and B improved the protective SiO2 phase grown during high-temperature oxidation and resulted in the formation of a continuous and dense oxide scale []. The addition of 6 at.% Ge in Nb-22Ti-12Si destabilised the Nb3Si, promoted the formation of Nb5Si3, significantly refined the microstructure and improved the high-temperature strength and room temperature fracture toughness respectively by about 88 and 19%, compared with the alloy without Ge []. The fracture toughness (KC, 3–point bend) of as-cast and heat-treated Nb-Ti-Si-Cr-Hf-Ge solid solution and silicide based alloys and the indentation toughness of the solid solution, Laves, and silicide phases have been reported []. The fracture toughness was not significantly changed by heat treatment and was about 10 MPa·m1/2 for alloys with more than 50 vol % silicide and Laves phases while the toughness of the solid solution ranged from 22 to 32 MPa·m1/2.

Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al was deposited on Ti-6Al-4V and Inconel 718 substrates in a rectangular shape of 10 mm transversely (X direction) and 40 mm longitudinally (Y direction). The Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al was deposited in two layers to a thickness of 1 mm. Each layer was deposited with five hatches, and the overlapping efficiency of the hatch was 40%. If the efficiency was lower than 30%, internal pores may have been generated, and the mechanical properties may have been reduced [,]. If the overlapping efficiency was too high, deformation and internal stress would occur, owing to the reduced productivity and thermal overlap. Figure 5 shows the schematic diagram of the overlapping efficiency. In the deposition of Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al, the laser power, scan speed, powder feed rate, and shield gas flow rate were used as deposition parameters. The experiment was conducted at room temperature and in a habitual state, and the DED equipment was sealed to block the inflow of air and prevent oxidation. Table 3 lists the deposition conditions, and Figure 6 shows the DED results of Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al.

reading.lever: Introduce ~6 at.% germanium to the titanium–nickel primary HEA to refine microstructure and stabilize protective phase formation.
reading.why: Ge addition has been shown to enhance high-temperature strength and oxidation resistance in Nb-Ti-Si alloys, suggesting similar benefits for Ti-Ni primary HEAs.
